items.title: Number of High-Intent Home Shoppers Dropped to a New Low Last Quarter as Stubborn Mortgage Rates Stymied Demand
items.description: Number of High-Intent Home Shoppers Dropped to a New Low Last Quarter as Stubborn Mortgage Rates Stymied Demand Buffalo, Hartford, Providence and San Francisco remain the most competitive markets Written by Treh Manhertz on November 23, 2026 The number of engaged home shoppers — Zillow users who save or share a for-sale listing — fell 4.8% from a year earlier to 3.5 per listing in the third quarter of 2026, the lowest level since Zillow began tracking the metric in 2023. Engaged shoppers per listing declined from last year in 44 of the 50 largest metro areas, led by Seattle, Washington, D.C. and Louisville. Four of the six major markets where engagement increased were in Florida. Luxury homes are drawing more than twice as many engaged shoppers per listing as starter homes. Home-buying demand last quarter hit the lowest level Zillow has tracked. Mortgage rates rose from July through September, leaving fewer serious shoppers in the market. The long-running inventory recovery is also spreading that dwindling demand across more homes. The number of engaged home shoppers per listing fell to 3.5 nationally in the third quarter of 2026. An engaged shopper is defined as a Zillow user who saved or shared a for-sale listing, signaling real interest beyond casual browsing. Agent activity is excluded from this analysis. The 3.5 engaged shoppers per listing last quarter is down 4.8% from a year earlier and the lowest level for any quarter since Zillow began tracking the metric in the second half of 2023. The pullback was widespread, with engagement down from last year in 44 of the 50 largest metro areas, although major Florida markets were an exception. Higher mortgage costs are the most likely driver of the drop in demand. Mortgage rates averaged 6.43% in Freddie Mac’s July 2 Primary Mortgage Market Survey , and rose to 7.28% by October 1. That jump in rates is enough to increase the monthly mortgage payment on a $400,000 home by nearly $200, from $2,008 to $2,189 (assuming a 20% down payment). Typical mortgage costs rose year over year in August, September and October, ending a 10-month streak of annual declines. Inventory keeps growing as shoppers pull back, helping bring down the number of engaged shoppers per listing. As of October, for-sale inventory has risen on an annual basis for 35 consecutive months, though it remains 14.4% below pre-pandemic norms. New listings have been a mixed bag, up on a year-over-year basis in just six of the past 12 months, suggesting the inventory buildup is more a result of homes staying on the market longer than a surge of new sellers. Nearly every major metro saw home shoppers pull back The pullback was widespread. Seattle saw the steepest drop in engaged shoppers per listing, down 17.1% from a year earlier. Washington, D.C. (-15.5%), Louisville (-14.3%), Salt Lake City (-13.7%) and Minneapolis (-13.4%) followed. Only six large metros posted gains, and four of them are in Florida: Jacksonville (+12.2%), Miami (+8.7%), Tampa (+4.2%) and Orlando (+0.8%). San Francisco (+5.1%) and Birmingham (+0.9%) were the others. Buffalo (6.7 engaged shoppers per listing), Hartford (6.2), Providence (6.1), San Francisco (6) and San Diego (5.2) had the most engagement last quarter. Despite its 8.7% year-over-year bounceback, Miami was one of the coolest markets with just 1.9 engaged shoppers per listing. Only Houston (1.6) had fewer. Luxury engagement holds steady while starter-home interest slides Luxury listings — homes among the top 5% most valuable in a given metro — typically drew 6.4 engaged shoppers last quarter, flat from a year earlier. Starter homes — homes in the 5th to 35th percentile of home values in a given metro — typically drew 2.9 engaged shoppers, down 8.2% year over year. This reflects the “K-shaped” housing market that has emerged. Economic headwinds such as slower hiring and rising inflation are prompting many households to delay major financial commitments like a home purchase. Higher-income households are in a different position. Stock market gains have boosted buying power, while higher mortgage rates have little impact on those who can make an all-cash purchase. Rental market is seeing spillover demand With for-sale demand waning, many would-be buyers appear to be turning to rentals instead. Nationally, rental demand is up 22.1% from a year earlier, according to Zillow’s October Rental Market Report . Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for apartments. The typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, about $360 less than the monthly cost of owning a single-family home with 20% down. items.title: $500M Data Center Debt Auction Fizzles, Leaving Dutch Bank To Shop For Buyers
items.description: An auction for $500M worth of data center debt stumbled out of the gate, and the lender is now at the door of buyers looking to make a deal. ING Bank Lackluster demand for the $500M worth of debt, including some backing high-profile data center projects in the U.S., led Dutch bank ING to abandon a so-called bids-wanted-in-competition process and turn to closing individual deals to clear the debt, Bloomberg reported Friday. The loans for sale are complicated and not easy to trade, and some buyers needed more time to evaluate the assets while ING was examining whether any of the offers it received through the bidding process were acceptable, Bloomberg reported, citing multiple anonymous sources who asked not to be identified to discuss private information. ING declined to comment when reached by Bisnow on Monday. The auction included a $25M piece of debt backing a massive joint venture called Project Jupiter from OpenAI and Oracle in New Mexico, but bids for the debt came in too low, sources told Bloomberg. There are other signs that investors have grown skeptical about Project Jupiter's scope and timeline. HSBC sold $300M in data center construction debt tied to Project Jupiter at less than 90 cents on the dollar earlier this month. The financing, part of an $18B package assembled by 20 banks, is backing a project that has faced widening community pushback and permitting hurdles. In September, Oracle sent a force majeure notice to the project's developer, Blue Owl Capital -owned Stack Infrastructure , looking to delay some rent payments due to setbacks at the project site. HSBC sold its $300M chunk immediately after the force majeure notice was sent, according to Bloomberg. ING was first reported to be shopping the $500M debt package earlier this month. The debt, a package of 12 loans, is also tied to data centers being developed by major operators like Vantage and CyrusOne . Some of the debt is associated with developments in Stargate , the sprawling Texas development project launched from the White House in January 2025. The attempted auction was reportedly the first to involve a portfolio made up solely of data center debt, and it comes as the broader artificial intelligence market tries to push through a sell-off and the sector-shaking news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had several affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang was ousted from the company he founded earlier this month only to be renamed to the top post Monday, sending the stock soaring more than 30%, although still down 20% from a month ago. The Magnificent 7 index, which tracks the seven mega-cap technology stocks, was up 8% on the news of Huang’s return in early trading Monday but remains down more than 4% over the last 30 days. Investors are beginning to question the run-up in tech stocks as the firms pour billions of dollars into the build-out of infrastructure to support as-yet-unproven AI systems. Anthropic , the maker of the Claude chatbot and a leading name in AI, went public last week at a valuation above $2T, but the stock was left out of the exuberance of Huang’s return to the fold Monday, with shares down more than 15% from the stock’s debut last week. items.description: Video: November 23, 2026, Economic and Housing Market Outlook By Joel Berner Nov 23, 2026 November 23, 2026 Reports and articles referenced: Featured Report Adults Living with Parents What’s Ahead Upcoming Realtor.com Economics Reports: Wednesday, November 25: 2026Q3 International Demand Report Thursday, November 26: Weekly Housing Data Recent Reports: Regional Adults at Home Tuesday, November 17: 2026Q3 New Construction Insights Quarterly Wednesday, November 18: October Rent Report Thursday, November, 19: AI Wealth and Bay Area Down Payments Thursday, November, 19: Anthropic IPO vs. Housing Wealth Thursday, November 19: Weekly Data Recent Indicators: Commentary on NAR Pending Home Sales – November 18, 2026 Commentary on New Residential Construction – November 18, 2026 Commentary on Freddie Mac Mortgage Rates – November 19, 2026 Housing data for download: https://www.realtor.com/research/data Video Script: Introduction: The holiday season is approaching, and many of you will be traveling home to visit your family to share meals, gifts, and quality time. But our research shows that some of you will not have to go far to see your parents, you may not even have to leave their house. That’s because a third of American adults under 35 years old still live in their parents’ home. High housing costs are keeping more young Americans in the nest, and I’ll get into how that breaks down across the country and what it means for the housing market. I'm Joel Berner, Senior Economist at Realtor.com sitting in for Chief Economist Danielle Hale , and this is The Weekly Housing Outlook , your guide to the best research and insights on the economy and housing market. Featured Reports Today’s featured report comes from Senior Economist Hannah Jones on where young adults are living with parents and what it says about the housing market. A record 25.2 million adults under 35 lived with their parents in 2025. That’s 33% of 18 to 34 year olds, or about one in three, and just shy of the all-time high of 33.6% set in 2020. Home prices are up at least 35% from pre-pandemic levels in every region, and high rents have made it tough for those who aren’t ready to buy. Living at home is how many young adults are bridging the gap between what they earn and what housing costs. But that national number hides a regional divide. The Northeast has the highest share at 36.9%, but it’s also the only region that’s improving. That rate is down 2.3 points from last year and is the lowest for the region since 2010. A wave of new apartments finished in 2024 and 2025 gave renters more options , and the region’s higher-wage industries likely helped more young adults make a move when conditions allowed. The rest of the country is heading the other way. The West is at 32.4%, the South at 32.3%, and the Midwest at 31.7%, and all three are up from last year. The Midwest now matches its pandemic peak, a sign that affordability pressure has reached markets long considered accessible. At the metro level, New York leads all major metros in terms of the share of young adults living at home at 41.3%, followed by Philadelphia and Miami at 38.6%. But the biggest changes are out West. Since the pandemic years, the share living at home is up 4.4 percentage points in Las Vegas, where home prices have climbed nearly 63% since 2019. It’s up 4.3 points in San Francisco and 3.9 in San Jose, where the return to the office likely pulled some young adults who had moved out back home. On the other end, Washington, DC, and Chicago saw the biggest improvements, with rates down 5.1 and 3.7 points. This doesn't just affect young adults in their early 20’s. In the West, nearly one in three at-home adults is between 25 and 34, which means working adults who haven’t been able to launch on their own. Every adult still in a childhood bedroom is a household that hasn’t formed yet. That pent-up housing demand isn't going away, and until affordability improves and more entry-level homes come to market, it will keep building. The Weekly Review: Now let’s look back at last week. Our research on free and clear homeownership gave an expected result, that the age cohort most likely to own their home outright is homeowners aged 75-plus. What we didn’t expect is that the free and clear ownership rate among seniors is falling, from 79.7% in 2010 to 71.3% in 2025. My colleague Jiayi Xu showed that more and more older Americans still have mortgages to pay, which adds to the stress of living on a fixed income. Meanwhile, outright ownership for American homeowners of all ages has risen in the past fifteen years, from 32.8% to 41.0%. Much like owners of homes with ultra-low mortgage rates from the pandemic era, free and clear ownership is subject to the lock-in effect. These owners are less likely to put their homes on the market when rates are high, as they would have to take on an expensive monthly payment if they decide to move. Next we took a look at the new construction segment. My quarterly New Construction Insights piece highlighted the trend that new construction asking prices have held remarkably steady, even as existing home prices have fallen throughout the year. One reason for those stable listing prices is that builders are offering buyers savings through reduced mortgage rate offers. Buyers of new construction can secure significant discounts on their mortgage rate relative to the market at large. The average new construction buyer in the third quarter of 2026 got a 5.01% initial mortgage rate compared to 6.15% for the average existing home buyer. That 114 basis point difference equates to monthly savings of $258 on a $400,000 home purchase with 10% down. It’s important to note that many of these mortgage rate buydowns are temporary, like the 3/2/1 buydown in which the rate in the first year is 3% below market, 2% below market in the second year, and 1% in the third year before returning to the standard rate in years four through thirty. items.title: The Geography of the Crowded Nest: Where Adults Are Living with Their Parents
items.description: The Geography of the Crowded Nest: Where Adults Are Living with Their Parents By Hannah Jones Nov 23, 2026 Key Takeaways A record 25.2 million adults under 35 live with their parents in 2025 — more than at any point on record, including the pandemic peak. At 33.0%, the share of young adults living at home is just below the all-time high of 33.6% set in 2020. Regionally, co-residence rates are highest in the Northeast, with 36.9% of 18-34 year-olds living with their parents, well-above the national rate. All other regions saw rates clustered just below the national norm. Though the Northeast sees the highest rate of co-residence, it is the only region that has seen significant improvement, with the lowest rate of adults at home since 2010. New York leads all major metros with 41.3% of young adults (18-34) living at home. Las Vegas and San Francisco have seen the sharpest post-pandemic deterioration, with co-residence rates rising more than 4 percentage points since the pandemic period. Nationally, a record-breaking 25.2 million adults under 35 are still under their parent’s roof , translating to roughly 1 in 3 young adults. The national figure masks a regional divide. In the Northeast, 36.9% of young adults live at home, the highest share of any region, followed by the West (32.4%), the South (32.3%) and the Midwest (31.7%). While the Northeast has seen modest improvement from its peak, the other three regions remain at or above pandemic-era highs. Home prices have risen sharply in every region since the pandemic, but the Northeast (+50.8%) and Midwest (+48.4%) have seen the steepest increases, with the West (+38.5%) and South (+34.8%) not far behind. With all four regions seeing price growth of at least 35% above pre-pandemic levels, the basic arithmetic of independent living has become harder to clear, and elevated rents have compounded the pressure for those not yet positioned to buy. For many young adults, staying home has become less a choice than a default, a way to keep options open until the gap between their incomes and housing costs narrows. Highest Rates, But Finally Easing: The Northeast Exception Over the last 25 years, the Northeast has seen an average 37.1% of young adults living at home, well above the national average of 30.2% in the same 25-year span. The other regions see lower rates, with 29.4% of young adults at home in the Midwest, and 28.5% in each the South and West. In 2025, the Northeast saw a co-residence rate of 36.9% for 18-34 year-olds. This is the lowest rate in the region since 2010, but still the highest in the country. 2025 Share of 18-34 Year Olds at Home by Region 2000-2025 Avg 2025 National 30.2% 33.0% (+0.6 pts YY) Northeast 37.1% 36.9% (-2.3 pts YY) South 28.5% 32.3% (+1.4 pts YY) Midwest 29.4% 31.7% (+1.4 pts YY) West 28.5% 32.4% (+0.5 pts YY) Some of the improvement in the Northeast can be attributed to the region having the furthest to fall to get in line with national norms. Additionally, rental supply relief helped young people in Northeast metros break out on their own . A wave of multifamily construction was completed in 2024 and 2025, offering options to renters in a market that suffers from very tight inventory. Simultaneously, the Northeast’s concentration of higher-wage industries like finance, healthcare, legal, and tech could mean that its at-home adults disproportionately had the income and credit history to act when mortgage rates briefly softened or new rental inventory arrived. The Northeast still sees very scarce inventory, which has kept upward pressure on prices, and will limit how much progress can be made towards national norms. Recent research from Realtor.com Economics found that the Northeast sees the biggest gap between new construction and housing demand , underscoring how difficult it is for young households to find an accessible place to live on their own. The Northeast’s 25–34 share (excluding 18-24 year-olds) of all at-home adults in the region has fallen from 33.4% in 2019 to 31.2% in 2025, suggesting that an older, more financially established cohort has exited. Put differently, early career professionals are a shrinking share of all at-home adults, suggesting these more established young adults have found avenues out of the house. The Rest of the Country Is Still Climbing While the Northeast sees high, but improving, co-residence, the rest of the country sees lower but rising rates of co-residence. The West sees an adult co-residence share of 32.4%, down slightly from the 2020 peak of 32.9%, but above the pre-pandemic norm near 30%. The South sees a similar trend with 32.2% of young adults living at home, even with the 2020 peak and above the pre-pandemic norm just below 30%. The Midwest sees the lowest share of adults living at home, with 31.7% of 18-34 year olds residing with their parents, also on-par with the region’s 2020 peak and above long-run norms. The Midwest’s rising co-residence rate tells a quieter but more persistent story. At 31.7%, it now matches its pandemic-era historical peak. Adults who would historically have launched independent households in Midwest cities by their late 20s increasingly aren’t, a signal that affordability pressure has reached markets long considered accessible. This growth can be seen especially clearly in the 25-34 cohort, where 14.8% of adults are living at home, the highest share in the region’s history. The South’s co-residence rate has climbed steadily from 26.6% in 2000 to 32.3% today. The rise has been fairly persistent, likely driven by rapid home price and rent appreciation in Sun Belt metros that hit local residents hard as those markets attracted higher-earning in-migrants and housing costs outpaced wage growth. items.title: Chicago multifamily sales activity nears decade high
items.description: Download the full report here.HighlightsA sustained pace of multifamily deliveries continued to apply upward pressure on vacancy in Chicago, with more than 3,800 units completed year to date. Rents held steady during the third quarter but remained above year-earlier levels.The vacancy rate inched higher during the third quarter, rising 10 basis points to 5.6%. In the past 12 months, the rate has risen by a total of 50 basis points.Asking rents went unchanged from the second quarter to the third quarter, remaining at $2,047 per month. Year over year, rents are up 2.3%.Multifamily sales activity accelerated in the third quarter following an already strong first half. The year-to-date median sale price is $238,400 per unit, while cap rates average approximately 6.0%.Chicago multifamily market overviewDeliveries in the Chicago multifamily market have held steady in recent months, with the pace of completions rising above last year’s lows but remaining below historical averages for the market. Downtown Chicago accounts for the largest share of units completed this year, although most new properties are dispersed across the outlying suburbs rather than concentrated in the urban core. Absorption also remains below typical levels, contributing to a 10 basis point increase in the market’s vacancy rate during the third quarter. Rents rose year over year in nearly every submarket, led by a 5.2% increase in Rogers Park. Vacancy trends were less favorable, with rates rising in most submarkets over the past year. Exceptions included Belmont to Montrose, The Loop, and Southwest Cook County, where vacancy declined from one year earlier.Multifamily sales activity has been elevated to this point in the year, with transactions spread widely across the metro area. Downtown stands out as the most active location, accounting for roughly 15% of total sales. By asset quality, Class B properties have driven the market, making up roughly half of all activity, while Class A and Class C properties have split the remaining transactions at a roughly even share. Pricing trends present a more nuanced picture. While pricing has shifted modestly overall, trends have varied in different vintages. Properties built since 2010 have accounted for 38% of the sales year to date, closely tracking levels recorded last year. Assets built in the 2010s have traded at a premium compared to the 2020s vintage assets. items.title: Single-Family Home Size Rising
items.description: Single-Family Home Size Rising November 23, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments New single-family home size had been falling since 2015 in response to declining affordability conditions. An exception occurred in 2021, when new home size increased as interest rates reached historic lows. However, as mortgage interest rates increased in 2022 and 2023 and affordability worsened, demand shifted back toward smaller homes. Now, this trend appears to be reversing again as entry-level construction has been weak and construction of larger homes have outperformed the overall market. According to third quarter 2026 data from the Census Quarterly Starts and Completions by Purpose and Design and NAHB analysis, median single-family square floor area was 2,164 square feet, down just a little from the prior quarter. Average (mean) square footage for new single-family homes increased to 2,455 square feet, a small increase year-over-year. On a one-year moving average basis, the average size of a new single-family home increased slightly to 2,433 square feet, while the median size was flat at 2,182. Since 2024 home size has trended higher as the upper end of the housing market has fared better than the entry level. items.title: FHA’s reverse mortgage book faces headwinds from home prices, fewer payoffs
items.description: The Federal Housing Administration ’s fiscal year 2026 actuarial report to Congress says the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage ( HECM ) reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile slice of the FHA's Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, showing that its stand-alone capital ratio dropped significantly in the wake of lower endorsement numbers over the past year. The report , released Nov. 16, found that the MMI Fund's overall capital ratio dropped slightly during the year ending Sept. 30, moving from 11.47% last year to 10.29% this year. The current figure, however, is roughly five times higher than fund's statutory minimum requirement of 2%. Looking exclusively at the HECM portfolio, the capital ratio was down significantly from 24.06% in FY 2025 to 5.43% in FY 2026. The FHA attributed this decline mainly to macroeconomic dynamics and program-specific cash flows. HECM remains profitable but capital buffer tightens The reverse mortgage portfolio, which accounts for less than 4% of the fund's insurance in force, is “much more sensitive to home prices,” the report explained. Slower home price appreciation and updated macroeconomic forecasts have increased projected losses for the HECM program. In addition, loan payoffs — which represent more favorable recovery outcomes than other disposition methods like foreclosures — have become less common and have pushed losses higher. The agency also noted that the HECM program “spent substantial capital resources on assignment claims in FY 2026, reducing available cash.” These claims, which are generated when FHA acquires loans that hit the 98% maximum claim amount threshold, are a known driver of volatility in the HECM book. They remain a key cost to monitor for reverse mortgage issuers and servicers . While the federally insured reverse mortgage portfolio is still in the black, the takeaway from the report is that its capital support can change rapidly due to shifts in home price appreciation, payoff behaviors and the frequency of assignment claims. These factors drive FHA policy decisions, as well as Ginnie Mae execution in the HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities ( HMBS ) market. HECM volume falls again, proprietary loans fill the gap The report illustrates that FHA-insured options remain central to the wider reverse mortgage market, even as volumes edge lower. In FY 2026, FHA insured 24,162 HECMs representing a maximum claim amount (MCA) of $12.81 billion. Endorsements were down about 14% from the 28,149 HECMs endorsed in FY 2025. MCA volume also fell from about $15.5 billion in 2025 to roughly $13.5 billion in 2026. But even with that pullback, the HECM program “remains a large part of the market,” according to the report. Historic data reinforces the sector’s structural shift. HECM endorsements peaked above 110,000 in 2009 with roughly $30.5 billion in MCA. Volumes have trended lower for more than a decade, with visible rebounds in 2020–2022 during a period of low interest rates and high home price growth. But higher rates and slower price growth since 2023 have softened demand. To fill the gap, lenders are focusing on proprietary reverse mortgages through their retail, wholesale and correspondent channels. The wider availability of these products has propelled a shift in market share as private-label loans accounted for more than 60% of reverse mortgage volume in September, according to New View Advisors . "I think that product diversity is great because we're able to serve more clients that the FHA product wouldn't handle," Jesse Allen , president of 55+ lending at Rate , told HousingWire 's Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD) at this month's National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo. He said these may be " mass affluent clients who have home values of $2 million or $3 million, and they really want to tap their equity without the debt service to achieve their goals," but they can also be clients who don't fit the HECM qualification requirements and are using reverse mortgage proceeds to consolidate debt. "This is another regulatory guideline NRMLA has advocated for. 'Hey, we're paying off consumer debts. Let's not count that toward the the qualification process.' Proprietary allows us to do that and HECM does not," Allen said. Portfolio characteristics, sensitivity to home prices FHA's FY 2026 report includes a dedicated HECM chapter that details borrower profiles and loan features. These include HECM loan purposes (such as home purchases versus refinancing of existing debt), payment plan options, interest rate types, borrower ages and maximum claim amounts and initial draws by recent borrower cohorts. The agency emphasizes that its actuaries model HECM cash flows separately from forward mortgages and explicitly stress-test the reverse portfolio under varying home price appreciation scenarios. Home price appreciation assumptions affect multiple levers across the program — including the available equity at the end of the loan, the size of recoveries through property sales and the loss severity tied to claims. Indirectly, home price growth can also impact payoff incentives. The report notes that waning price growth in 2026 had an “outsized negative impact” on HECM capital compared with forward mortgages. This underscores why even modest regional or national home price corrections are more consequential for HMBS investors and issuers than for traditional mortgage-backed securities . The stand-alone capital ratio of 5.43% for the HECM portfolio suggests that FHA still has room to absorb stress, but far less cushion than in the prior three years when the ratio ranged between roughly 16% and 25%. It also may create more difficulty for industry advocates in their push to reduce upfront mortgage insurance premiums. In September, Ginnie Mae President Joe Gormley told RMD that the Trump administration is "very comfortable" with the current mortgage insurance structure for FHA single-family loans and reverse mortgages. items.title: Stuck: How a frozen housing market is hitting buyers, sellers and the economy
items.description: 'The scary part' It all has Ryan Deighan, who wants to buy a home, wondering if he ever will. "I genuinely don't know, and that's the scary part," he said. Deighan and his wife have been renting in Boston for six years. He is a chiropractor; she works in private equity. Even with a combined salary of more than $200,000 a year, he says they're stuck. Boston chiropractor Ryan Deighan is unsure if he'll ever be able to buy a home. CNBC "Making what I am and what my wife makes, it just feels like we're on paper doing well, but it feels like we are still kind of fighting to put down certain amounts toward a house," Deighan said. Being priced out of homeownership, he said, is changing what he called his "checklist" of how he once pictured his future. "You graduate college, you find someone, you get married, you have the home with the white picket fence and the dog, and then the kids," he said. "That just looks a little different for us." Sellers are stuck, too The numbers don't just affect would-be buyers. They are hitting sellers, too. Robin Welch has been living in her Cleveland-area home for more than 20 years. Her children are now grown and moved out. She would like to downsize to a condominium, but the math doesn't make sense — in part, because her current interest rate is much lower than any new rate she could get. This has been dubbed the mortgage "lock-in effect." "It actually costs more money to buy less of a home," said Welch. "I would have to pay into an HOA, which would be another monthly expense on top of increased property taxes and increased interest rate." Welch has also done upgrades to her home over the years and doesn't want to have to start doing that on another home. Subscribe here to get access today . Welch is part of why the housing turnover rate, which is how often homes get new owners, has now dropped to just 3.8% a year, well below the 5% rate in the decade following the financial crisis, according to Cotality. In addition, the national mobility rate, which is how often people move from region to region, has been falling for two years. It now sits at 8.3%, down from 11.1% a decade ago, according to Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies tabulations of U.S. Census Bureau data. Mobility hit a high of nearly 18% in the late 1980s. "It's largely because of the interest lock-in effect, but also because of home prices just being so high," said Riordan Frost, senior research analyst at Harvard's JCHS. "Those things combined have made it hard both for existing homeowners to move and for people to get into homeownership." Americans have nearly $35 trillion of their wealth locked up in housing, a record high , according to Cotality. But the slowdown in the housing market, Frost said, impacts the accumulation, handover and use of that wealth. It also affects the labor market. "Any kind of potential job would have to really outweigh … the price of taking that mortgage with a higher rate, or the price of moving, or the price of getting into a higher rent unit," Frost said. The wealth gap between homeowners and renters now is nothing short of massive. The most recent survey of consumer finances last year by the Federal Reserve showed that the median homeowner net wealth is about 43 times the median renter net wealth. "It has kind of knock-on effects for the rest of the economy. It has effects on the labor market and how good of a match we can get between employees and employers. It has an effect on education. It has an effect on just GDP growth," said Zhao. Buyers back out When homes aren't selling and people aren't moving, those who work in that business are stuck as well. The entire housing ecosystem is churning much more slowly, and the sudden jump in mortgage rates is causing deals to fall apart. "Right after Labor Day, we went live with a bunch of listings. They all went under contract over the asking price," said Dana Bull, a real estate agent in the Boston suburbs. But then rates spiked. "It was a shock to the system," Bull said. "I think all of them came back on the market. We fell out of contract." Asked if she is seeing colleagues leaving the market, she answered: "People are thinking about it. It's tough." Dana Bull, a real estate agent in the Boston suburbs. CNBC The economy has lost close to 2,000 jobs in real estate and leasing over the past year and 4,400 jobs in residential construction, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Jobs in the mortgage industry have been falling since June and are down 38% since their last peak in the second quarter of 2021, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. That was when mortgage rates were less than half what they are today. Shant Banosian, president of Rate and the top mortgage originator in the U.S. by dollar volume, said his business is down about 30% this past year. "Whenever change happens quickly, there's a slowdown," said Banosian, who has been in the business for 23 years. "It requires more of us to go out and advise, educate and guide. So, what I experienced was I just needed to spend more time on marketing, branding, relationship building. The conversations are longer because people want more information to try to navigate this market." Bull agrees. She said her job has gotten harder as well. "We've done double the work this year, having homes go under contract, fall out of contract, putting them back under agreement, but definitely more negotiating," she said. "That's sort of my plea to both buyers and sellers: We need to get back to a space where we're comfortable negotiating." items.title: Which real estate business model is king in today’s slower market?
items.description: Which real estate business model is king in today’s slower market? by Emily Marek November 23, 2026 Phoenix Agent spoke to brokerage leaders D. Patrick Lewis, Nicholas Yale, Amanda Thomason, Todd Sumney, Oleg Bortman, Katrina Barrett, Kristina Watson and Sherri Monteith to determine the optimal real estate business model for today's slower market. Phoenix’s real estate market isn’t what it used to be. Long gone are the days when new agents flooded the industry to sell multiple homes a month to buyers with sub-4% mortgage rates. Things are different now — and yet, people still need Realtors. People still need to relocate, or size up their square footage, or adjust to their family’s changing needs. And the agents who will stand the test of time are the ones who are still finding ways to work for their clients, despite current market conditions. But what does that look like on the business end? Is there a specific brokerage model or agent blueprint that works best in today’s slower market ? Phoenix Agent spoke with eight prominent Phoenix-area brokerage leaders to discuss the business strategies that cultivate the most success for agents — and their clients. Here's what they had to say. Oleg Bortman, Co-Founder, The Brokery Oleg Bortman said that boutique brokerages — particularly those with split, percentage-based commission models — are best positioned to succeed in today’s market. “When you have a flat fee or a very, very low monthly fee or transaction fee, the broker themselves cannot provide any value other than straight-up being the cheapest on the market,” Bortman said. “The boutique firms or independents that take a split typically have more back-end support … So in a market where homes are taking a much longer time to sell, and you need more than just a pulse to sell a house, you have to have a brand that’s very strong to differentiate yourself in a market that’s flooded with Realtors.” Bortman added that AI is not the answer to marketing woes. “Artificial intelligence is not going to be the answer to everything in order to save money,” he explained. “Most agents don’t like to spend any money, so they need to have the local brand that’s strong and professionals doing their marketing. Most agents are either good at sales or good at marketing, but they can’t typically do both.” While local brokerages are best positioned to succeed in today’s market, conversely, Bortman said downstream brokerage models are antiquated systems. Those models often require agents to act as Realtors and recruiters at the same time — and it’s more beneficial for agents to change their mindset and pick a lane, Bortman said. “You can’t be a good recruiter, a good Realtor, a good business owner, all at once. And when you think you’re being a good recruiter, you’re still depending on someone else’s production,” Bortman said. “So when a market gets tighter, like we’re seeing now, even if you have 50 or 100 people downstream that used to sell one house a month, now they’re selling one every four months. You’re not going to get any residual income. It’s forcing them to go back to selling houses and not just recruiting.” Bortman also cautioned agents away from low-cap commission splits, which he said provide very little incentive for business owners to put money back into their business, let alone their agents’ businesses. Instead, he said, find a firm that invests in agents’ potential success. “Find a firm that believes in training and coaching,” Bortman said. “You want to go to a firm where the more you sell, the smaller the split comes, but you still pay something into the split because then the owner has an incentive for you to sell more real estate because then you’re [both] making more money.” Todd Sumney, Chief Industry Officer, HomeSmart Teams are growing — but not in the way people might think, said Todd Sumney . Specifically, Sumney pointed to local, independent brokerages that affiliate with large, technology-driven companies like HomeSmart and begin operating as large teams. By affiliating with a large, national brokerage, Sumney said, those smaller brokerages are getting rid of their liability and gaining access to resources like a broker team, paperwork team, closing team, payment team, technology and transaction-management software to help them manage their transactions. “Instead of doing all that plus running a business, now they can just focus on training their agents, coaching their agents, helping them with marketing, recruiting and retaining,” he explained. Sumney specifically pointed to NEXT , a large-scale HomeSmart team led by Phil Sexton that operates as a sort of “brokerage within a brokerage.” “[Sexton] wants to be the back-end support for individual agents and teams under his team,” Sumney said. “NEXT is doing all the marketing, transaction management, video work, marketing creation, media buys, materials and transaction management, and he’s using AI to build efficiency and really support these agents.” That's a valuable model for agents who want to be out in the field, working with their clients, rather than worrying about social media posts or writing scripts. “The teams that are successful now are taking that burden, both administrative and marketing, off the agent,” Sumney said. However, Sumney said that regardless of which brokerage agents find themselves aligned with, it’s important to remember that a slower market doesn’t automatically mean a less successful business. “Great agents don’t let the number of transactions in the market actually dictate their production,” Sumney said. “Real estate is about serving our customers, helping them and engaging them, and not expecting anything in return. items.title: Flat Conditions for Built-to-Rent Construction
items.description: Flat Conditions for Built-to-Rent Construction November 23, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments Single-family built-for-rent (SFBFR, or built-to-rent (BTR)) construction was flat for the third quarter of 2026, just prior to enactment of legislation that, fortunately, did not include harmful financing rules for BTR housing. A rebound for the sector may be in store given priced-out homebuyers and certainty regarding financing rules. According to NAHB’s analysis of data from the Census Bureau’s Quarterly Starts and Completions by Purpose and Design , there were approximately 19,000 single-family built-for-rent ( SFBFR ) starts during the third quarter of 2026. This is up 6% from the third quarter of 2025 (18,000). Over the last four quarters, 69,000 such homes began construction, which is flat from the estimated BTR starts for the prior four quarter period (also 69,000). The BTR market is a source of inventory amid challenges regarding housing affordability and down payment requirements in the for-sale market, particularly during a period when a growing number of people want more space and a single-family structure. Single-family built-for-rent construction differs in structural characteristics compared to other newly-built single-family homes, particularly with respect to home size. Given the relatively small size of this market segment, the quarter-to-quarter movements typically are not statistically significant. The current four-quarter moving average of market share (just above 7%) is nonetheless higher than the historical average of 2.7% (1992-2012). Importantly, as measured for this analysis, the estimates noted above include only homes built and held by the builder for rental purposes. The estimates exclude homes that are sold to another party for rental purposes, which NAHB estimates may represent another three to five percent of single-family starts based on industry surveys. The Census data note an elevated share of single-family homes built as condos (non-fee simple), with this share averaging about 3% over recent quarters. Some, but certainly not all, of these homes will be used for rental purposes. Additionally, it is theoretically possible that some single-family built-for-rent units are being counted in multifamily starts, as a form of “horizontal multifamily,” given that these units are often built on a single plat of land. However, spot checks by NAHB with permitting offices continue to indicate no evidence of this data issue occurring. With the onset of the Great Recession and declines in the homeownership rate , the share of built-for-rent homes increased in the years after the recession. While the market share of SFBFR homes is small, it has clearly expanded. items.title: Beyond commission splits: How wellness benefits give brokerages a recruiting edge
items.description: By many estimations, real estate professionals are facing the most challenging housing market in recent memory in 2027 . Unlike in the past, many will be doing so with access to more resources than ever designed to ensure they are feeling healthy, at the peak of their game and ready to tackle whatever the 2027 housing market throws at them. This is because over the past year, several brokerages announced a variety of wellness programs and health insurance opportunities they are now offering to agents, who as independent contractors, typically do not have access to things like insurance through their brokerage. Since the start of 2026, ENRG Realty , Compass International Holdings , Equity Union Real Estate and John R. Wood Properties have announced the launch of health insurance or wellness benefits initiatives. “We were founded on Maslow Hierarchy of Needs, so health insurance fits right in with some of the core basic values that we need to provide to our agents so they can be successful and thrive,” Erinn Nobel, the co-founder and president of ENRG Realty and a HousingWire Woman of Influence award winner, said. “In order for our agents to function at a high level, they can’t be sitting at home worried about an illness or being able to pay their bills because they don’t have health coverage. It is a foundational offering and a benefit for us to be able to provide it for our agents.” Nobel said that while some Realtor boards or associations offer health insurance, there is often just one policy option, something she experienced first hand after moving to Alaska from Washington state. “It was great to be able to access insurance through our board, but there was only one plan, so you couldn’t shop around,” Nobel said. “It just didn’t sit well with me that my options were so limited.” A similar experience with challenges accessing insurance for his family is also what inspired Harma Hartouni , the CEO of Equity Union Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, to begin providing his agents with access to group-style health coverage options, including a nationwide PPO network, through a partnership with Trident BPO . When he approached the executive team about launching this initiative, Hartouni said they were a bit divided as to whether or not they should do this. “Some thought the agents wouldn’t care, but some of our managers thought it was great,” Hartouni said. “Ultimately, our agents are our clients, and I knew that if these people were not healthy or not in a clear mindset in this challenging market, they would not function well.” In the current uncertain economic environment, Hartouni added that the offering has also provided many agents, who previously had access to insurance through a spouse who lost their job, a level of peace of mind that they couldn’t previously provide. “The consistent feedback from agents is that they are saving money and are able to see better doctors,” Hartouni said. After rolling out the program, Nobel said she and her team received countless messages from agents saying thank you. Beyond better serving existing agents, Nobel said the program also helped ENRG Realty with agent recruitment. “It has become an attraction magnet for us. Savvy agents that have been in the industry for a while are starting to really compare brokerages and look at what benefits they get from each brokerage and the different values they provide,” Nobel said. “If an agent already has access to health insurance through a spouse or partner, then this may not convey the same value as it would to a self-employed single mom who would love to have access to health care.” Hartouni has also noticed the agent recruitment benefits of offering health insurance. “The smart broker is looking for producing agents that are in the middle of their career, where they still have plenty of years left in the business to learn and grow, but have already begun to establish themselves,” he said. “But these agents often have families to think about and how can we help them have one less thing to worry about? items.title: Cost cutting is not cost reduction; builders and trades face a test
items.description: A reliable estimate of the tariff burden on a typical newly built American home puts the cost at $12,919, or about $4.88 per square foot. That is before accounting for broader inflation in construction labor, transportation, services and other inputs that homebuilders must absorb while trying to make their homes affordable to increasingly price-sensitive customers. This informed baseline calculation of tariff impact at the new-home level, developed by homebuilding supply-chain consultancy Strategem through its Strategy Pulse Pro platform, updates the National Association of Home Builders ' April 2025 builder-reported tariff-cost estimate of $10,900 to reflect subsequent trade-policy changes. The model distributes tariff exposure across 17 material categories, with hardware and fasteners, steel products, lumber, cabinets, windows and aluminum accounting for some of the highest estimated costs. By its nature, Strategem’s tally is a modeled cost burden, not a direct measure of tariffs paid on every home or of the amount passed through to buyers. Still, it illustrates a difficult dilemma for homebuilders, and one none of them can simply avoid: Costs imposed upstream cannot necessarily be recovered downstream. And in that downstream market, households increasingly lack the financial capacity or confidence to buy homes at the prices builders need to charge. That predicament, predictable in a falling market, is a reflexive homebuilding firm response that reverberates through homebuilding’s wider ecosystem like a bad-trip flashback. Homebuilders are looking to their suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and trade contractors to shoulder more of the financial pain. It's a law of dismal science physics during a downturn: Wringing a bit of margin improvement by most builders means squeezing suppliers' margins into further negative territory. The danger is that some builders may, and often do, push their business partners beyond what they can reasonably absorb. This tactic, seductive as it may seem as a way to claw back input cost reductions, mostly serves as a temporary fix. Ultimately, such quick fixes undermine the very production capacity, service reliability, and competitive supplier pools they will need to survive the downturn and recover. The shock absorbers are wearing thin Homebuilders have spent much of the past two years using price reductions, mortgage-rate buydowns and other incentives to preserve sales velocity. Those concessions have helped sustain production, but they have also eroded the earnings cushion – the “shock absorber” – that previously allowed many builders to absorb rising costs without substantially disrupting operations. The squeeze is occurring on both sides of builders' income statements. According to NAHB's November 13 analysis of Producer Price Index data, goods used in new residential construction rose 9.8% year over year in October, while service inputs increased 11.3%. The combined input index rose 10.4%, including a 5.8% increase in building-material prices. These are input-price indexes, not equivalent percentage increases in the total cost of constructing a house. Still, they reveal why slowing demand has not delivered the broad-based cost relief builders might otherwise expect. The pressure is particularly difficult for smaller builders and suppliers with limited financial reserves. They must keep enough business flowing to cover fixed costs while protecting the margins and working capital required to remain viable. When cost savings aren't really savings Ken Pinto, a longtime homebuilding strategic-sourcing executive and co-founder of Strategem, and a friend of The Builder's Daily , believes the industry risks conflating two fundamentally different types of cost reduction. Purchasing departments are reporting savings from increasingly competitive bidding, he says, but those reductions often come from suppliers sacrificing profitability rather than from lasting improvements in how homes are built. "When you reduce costs by going out to bid, going out to bid, going out to bid, you're not taking cost out of the supply chain; you're taking margins out," Pinto says. This self-preservatory instinct among homebuilding business decision-makers has important, potentially risky, consequences. A trade contractor who accepts a lower price to keep crews working may provide immediate relief to a builder's direct costs, but the underlying costs of labor, transportation, insurance, equipment, and materials may remain unchanged. When demand eventually recovers, those concessions may disappear. More troubling, some suppliers may not survive long enough to participate in the recovery. Pinto points to manufacturers facing higher costs for steel, copper and resin-based products while struggling to secure corresponding price increases. Their customers may be able to delay accepting price increases, but the underlying costs do not disappear simply because builders refuse to pay them. The resulting margin compression can become unsustainable. A fragile supply chain beneath the surface Conversations with homebuilding purchasing professionals suggest that the opportunities for further reductions vary considerably by category. Some material suppliers remain willing to compete aggressively for market share, particularly in areas where slower construction activity has created excess capacity. But trade contractors face different circumstances. Years of declining production volume have already weakened some local subcontractor businesses. In some markets, established trade firms have closed, while others struggle with cash flow, payment disputes and mechanics' liens. At the same time, immigration enforcement has reduced labor availability in trades including framing, concrete, masonry, roofing, electrical work and painting. items.title: REIT Sells 400-Unit Arlandria Apartment Community For $69M
items.description: UDR has offloaded a suburban D.C. asset that it had owned for a quarter of a century. The REIT sold Presidential Greens, a 1930s-era garden-style community in what is called Arlandria — a Northern Virginia neighborhood on the border of Arlington and Alexandria — after holding on to it since 2002. Google Maps The Presidential Gardens multifamily community at 3904 Executive Ave. in Alexandria, Virginia A joint venture between Blackfin Real Estate Investors and JSB Capital Group purchased the 396-unit property at 3904 Executive Ave. for $69M, the buyers and Berkadia announced Monday. UDR revealed in its third-quarter earnings report earlier this month that the property was under contract for the disclosed price. UDR didn’t respond to Bisnow ’s request for comment. The REIT, which owns 9,129 units in greater D.C., according to its Q3 supplemental , originally paid $30M for Presidential Greens. The buyers said in a press release that the asset benefits from D.C.-area multifamily deliveries “slowing considerably,” the need for attainable housing for workers like teachers and public servants, and the property's proximity to employment nodes. The purchase represents Blackfin and JSB’s 13th transaction together, Blackfin co-founder and Managing Partner Doug Root said, adding that it had been a few years since the last one. “We have been focused on trying to find a well-located, strong cash flowing asset for our next investment,” he said in the release. “Recent market conditions have made that more challenging but the location and profile of Presidential Greens fit our objective to a tee.” Berkadia represented the seller and secured financing for the buyer. Senior Managing Director Brian Crivella led the investment sales team, and Managing Director Brian Gould and Senior Managing Director Patrick McGlohn led the mortgage banking team. Truist provided acquisition financing, the terms of which weren’t disclosed. “Presidential Greens represents a compelling investment opportunity in one of Northern Virginia's most established rental markets,” Crivella said in a separate release from the brokerage. “With nearly 400 apartments in a highly accessible Alexandria location, the property offers scale, a strong occupancy history and enduring housing demand — attributes that continue to attract capital.” Northern Virginia accounted for 70% of the $4.2B in multifamily investment sales that occurred across the D.C. metro during the first three quarters of the year, according to Northmarq . This year's multifamily sales volume has already surpassed the figure for the entirety of 2025. items.description: The ongoing Chicago Bears stadium saga has taken another turn, with the team reportedly negotiating with a suburb of its hometown for taxpayer-backed funding. The team, state lawmakers and the government of Arlington Heights are discussing a plan that would use local tax revenue generated by a proposed $3.5B stadium and nearby properties to back tax-exempt construction bonds, Crain’s Chicago Business reports . Parking and amusement taxes are among the potential sources targeted for revenue, although the amount is unknown. items.description: Buying a home comes with enough expenses already. Between inspections , title insurance , closing costs, and a stack of paperwork that seems to grow every day, it's easy to lose track of what you're paying for. But what if your employer could help cover some of the legal bills? It's a possibility many homebuyers may overlook during open enrollment, when employees are typically comparing health insurance premiums and retirement benefits rather than thinking about hiring a lawyer. Employer-sponsored legal plans, offered through companies such as LegalShield , MetLife and ARAG , can provide access to attorneys for a modest monthly fee. A real estate attorney can review a purchase agreement, make sure inspection and financing contingencies actually protect the buyer, check the deed and title, examine mortgage documents, and represent a buyer at closing. Depending on the plan, some or all of that may be covered. Jago Gavin , a LegalShield representative who works with employer groups, tells Realtor.com® that the real value is having someone to consult before signing something you might not fully understand. "The law is not logical; it's legal," Gavin says. That's relevant when buying a house , where an unfamiliar contract provision can have expensive consequences. Gavin recalls a LegalShield member whose attorney spotted a potentially unfavorable mediation clause in real estate paperwork and recommended changing it before the buyer signed. The potential savings can run from hundreds to thousands of dollars. But there's a catch: Not all legal plans offer the same services, and buyers need to know what they're getting before signing up. Legal help for about $20 a month? Group legal plans work much like other voluntary workplace benefits. Employees pay a monthly premium, usually through payroll deductions, in exchange for access to specified legal services. The price can be surprisingly affordable. In a review of publicly available employee benefits documents, Realtor.com found a plan offered to employees of financial technology company Fiserv through MetLife for $15.50 monthly. LegalShield's published employer plans generally cost about $19 to $25 a month, depending on the coverage and employer. That's roughly $186 to $300 annually, potentially less than the cost of a single consultation with a private attorney. The plans typically provide access to participating law firms that handle matters ranging from contract reviews and consumer disputes to estate planning. Some cover specific services in full, while others offer discounted rates for legal work outside the plan. Loading... ContractsCounsel , an online marketplace connecting clients with attorneys, reports that lawyers on its platform charged an average flat fee of $620 to review a real estate purchase agreement, based on completed projects. Compare that with LegalShield's published Choice plan, which costs $21.95 monthly, or $263.40 over a year. If an employee uses the plan for comparable document-review work without additional charges, the potential savings could be about $350. But reviewing a contract and representing someone throughout a real estate transaction are two very different services. LegalShield's published employer-plan documents include certain residential mortgage-document reviews but specifically exclude an attorney's attendance at closing. Documents must also be provided at least five business days before the scheduled closing. Other plans offer broader coverage. An ARAG legal plan available to University of California employees, for example, pays participating attorneys for covered services that include reviewing and preparing home purchase documents and attending a closing. California doesn't generally require attorneys at residential closings, but the benefit illustrates how coverage can extend beyond reviewing paperwork. The MetLife plan offered to Fiserv employees also lists home purchases and sales among its covered services. MetLife plan descriptions published by several other employers go further, listing deeds, boundary and title disputes, and property tax assessments—handy if a new owner wants to challenge a tax bill after the purchase. Employees should still check precisely what their particular plan includes. And even comprehensive coverage won't eliminate ordinary closing expenses. Buyers are generally still responsible for title insurance, recording fees, taxes and other third-party charges. Is there a downside to using a plan attorney? New York real estate attorney Adam Leitman Bailey sees the obvious appeal: lower costs. But he questions whether attorneys with busy, established practices have much incentive to participate in programs requiring them to accept reduced fees. For a relatively straightforward transaction, that might not matter much, he says. But complicated purchases can be another story. "When something goes wrong, and this is the biggest investment of your lifetime, you'd better believe that you should be hiring the best attorney you can," Bailey tells Realtor.com. That doesn't mean attorneys participating in group plans are necessarily less qualified. It does mean buyers should ask about their experience, particularly if a transaction involves title disputes, unusual contract provisions, or other complications. Availability matters, too. Gavin acknowledges that LegalShield sometimes encounters coverage gaps in rural areas, where the nearest participating firm may be hours away. items.title: Mount Street Establishes New Dallas Hub, Buys $1.4B Servicing Business
items.description: London-based finance firm Mount Street Group has hired a team of seasoned primary and special servicing professionals to establish a Dallas hub. The expansion deal will add almost $1.4B of assets to its approximately $30B U.S. servicing book, according to an announcement on Monday . The group, led by former Credit Suisse credit chief Paul Smyth, will oversee the firm’s U.S. securitized products, collateralized loan obligation and special servicing business. Wikimedia Commons/Mx. Granger Mount Street Group's London headquarters at 100 Wood St. “The securitized products and special servicing markets require experience, judgment and a disciplined approach to execution,” Smyth, who was named managing director and head of securitized products in the U.S., said in a statement. “Mount Street’s platform gives us the ability to bring those capabilities to clients at greater scale, supported by a strong global infrastructure and a clear commitment to growth in the U.S. market." The team is made up of executives from Broadsword Investors, co-founded by Smyth, and Goldersun Loan Servicing, both Dallas-based firms. The servicing book was acquired from Goldersun, according to a Mount Street spokesperson. Throughout his 40-year career, Smyth has managed more than $55B in loan resolutions. He served as Credit Suisse ’s global chief credit officer and president of Greystone ’s special servicing portfolio before starting his own specialty finance firm. Broadsword was founded alongside Cary Williams, who will also join Mount Street, focusing on new client initiatives and asset management. Mount Street’s new team also includes Joe Beggins, who was CEO of General Electric Capital Loan Services and GEMSA Loan Services, the subsequent commercial mortgage servicing joint venture between GE and CBRE . Beggins has held leadership positions at other CRE firms since, including managing member of Goldersun. He will oversee asset management and process enhancements for investors at Mount Street. Goldersun CEO Terry Clay will move to Mount Street, where he will serve as head of the surveillance and reporting team. He previously worked at Hudson Advisors. John Roach, who worked with Smyth at other companies, including Greystone, will lead the Dallas team's primary servicing and CLO operations components. In a statement, Rawle Howard, head of Mount Street USA, said the addition of the new team “marks a meaningful acceleration of Mount Street’s U.S. growth strategy.” “Their market credibility, technical expertise and deep experience across securitized products, B-Piece investing, CMBS, special servicing and asset management are highly complementary to our existing platform and will immediately enhance the depth of service we can provide to clients,” Howard said. “This transaction is not just about adding scale; it is about adding the right people, capabilities and leadership to support the next phase of our U.S. growth.” Founded in 2013, Mount Street has more than €163B of assets under administration and €31.9B in assets under valuation, or roughly $177.5B and $34.7B, respectively. It employs more than 200 people across Europe and the U.S. The global third-party loan servicing and credit management business established its North American branch in 2017. Mount Street USA is headquartered in Atlanta. items.title: Mortgage headlines aren’t as big a concern as your cost per closing
items.description: If you run a real estate team, several weeks ago you probably saw and heard the chatter about potential rate hikes as high as 9% in 2027. I understand why it spread. Freddie Mac had the 30-year fixed at 7.28% on Oct. 1, up from 6.01% in February and the Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023. If everything moves the wrong way at once, 9% could sound possible. The Real Estate Agent Facebook groups were bubbling about this in the comments. It is likely causing some anxiety for many agents. It helps to look at what it would actually take. Cotality's chief economist, Selma Hepp, raised 9% on CNBC as a worst case, not a forecast. HousingWire's Logan Mohtashami laid out the math: the 10-year would have to push past 6%, and mortgage spreads would have to widen well beyond the roughly 2% they sit at today. That requires a hot economy, oil prices that stay high and a Fed that keeps hiking past what markets expect, all lasting well into next year. September's jobs report showed 29,000 new jobs, which already works against the hot-economy part. So I wouldn't plan around 9%. I also wouldn't plan around rates falling back to 6% anytime soon. The Fed's own projections show no cuts in 2027, and the Mortgage Bankers Association expects rates to stay close to where they are. The real problem is quieter A crash needs forced sellers, and we don't have many. Homeowners with a mortgage carry an average loan-to-value of about 44%, and only around 2% are underwater, according to Cotality . That isn't 2008. What we do have is fewer deals. In early October, pending sales were about 10% less than the year before, and purchase applications were down 14%. Those applications turn into closings 30 to 90 days later, so a lot of teams have been looking at a softer first quarter. At today’s rate, the payment that covered a $400,000 loan in February covers about $357,000 now. Same buyer, same budget, about 11% less loan. Prices mostly hold, and the deal count shrinks. I think of 2027 as a consolidation year rather than a crash year. Why this is a cost-per-closing problem In August, I wrote here that cost-per-lead is the wrong number to run a team on, and that cost-per-closed deal is the one that tells you the truth. A slow year is when that stops being a philosophy and turns into a real potential problem. Most of what a team spends to generate business is fixed. The ad campaign, vendor contracts, the ISA hours and the coaching all get billed whether deals close or not. When conversion falls, none of those invoices get smaller. Say a team spends $6,000 a month on lead generation and closes 12 deals a quarter from it. That's $1,500 per closing. Then buyer conversion slips, and the same spend produces nine closings. Now each closing costs $2,000. Nothing on the invoice changed, and every deal got a third more expensive. That's the exposure I'd worry about: a cost structure built for a 6.5% market, running in a 7.5% one. The gap between a team that knows its number and one that doesn't gets much wider when volume drops. How to hedge your team or brokerage You can't control the 10-year Treasury. These are the things you can control though: Find your cost per closing by source. Add up everything you spend on each lead source, including ad spend, platform and referral fees, ISA time and software, and divide it by the closed transactions that source produced over the last 12 months. Use closings, not appointments or signed agreements. Most team leads I talk to have never broken this out by source, and the answer usually surprises them. Stress-test it at a lower deal count. Run the same numbers assuming 20% fewer closings. Any source that ends up costing more per closing than your net is one to fix or cut now, while you still have room to choose. Shift your mix toward sellers and your sphere. Buyers are the first to stall when rates jump. Sellers still have to move for new jobs, divorces, estates, and growing families, whatever the rate happens to be, and your past clients are sitting on real equity. If most of your pipeline is buyer leads, 2027 will hurt more than it should. Lengthen your nurture instead of cutting it. The buyer who is priced out at 7.5% may be ready at 6.75%. If your follow-up ends at 90 days, someone else gets that deal if rates turn, and you end up paying for the same lead twice. Give your agents training so they can handle these clients. Don’t promise rates will fall. Understand the concern first, then help the buyer evaluate actual numbers without treating a forecast as a fact. The teams that come out ahead 2023 had the fewest existing-home sales since 1995. The teams I watched hold up through it weren't the ones that guessed right about rates. They were the ones that knew what each closing cost them and kept moving money toward what was working. There will be another very scary hot topic after this one, and another after that. The best hedge against all of them is the same: know your cost per closing, and build a pipeline that doesn't depend on buyers feeling good about rates. Robyn Thompson DeSantos is the founder and CEO of Ascension Group, a business solutions and management company for real estate team leaders and brokers. items.description: Weidner Apartment Homes Spends $91M on Denver Apartment Property Kirkland, Washington-based Weidner Apartment Homes has acquired Patten Gray , a 250-unit luxury apartment building in Denver's Golden Triangle neighborhood, for $90.75 million, or $363,000 per unit. The property was sold by a joint venture of Rockefeller Group and Summit Capital Venture Partners. Completed in 2024, the 13-story, Class-A high-rise is built of Type I all-concrete construction. It is located at 370 W. 12th Ave., in the city’s Golden Triangle area, close to downtown Denver, Cherry Creek, and local parks. The community boasts a Walk Score of 96 and a Bike Score of 98. Apartments include high ceilings, quartz countertops, and designer finishes. Building amenities feature a rooftop sky deck, a fifth-floor saltwater pool, an outdoor sauna, a fitness center, coworking spaces, a pet spa, EV parking, and ground-floor retail anchored by Flora coffee and cocktail bar. The acquisition marks Weidner's first investment in the Denver metropolitan area since its 2015/16 portfolio disposition. Courtney Crowder and Jack Kachadurian of Newmark represented the sellers. items.title: Martin Commercial Properties Lands $15M in Construction Money for Phoenix Development
items.description: Martin Commercial Properties Lands $15M in Construction Money for Phoenix Development Martin Commercial Properties' has secured $15 million in construction financing for the ground-up development of a 102,302-square-foot Class A flex industrial project in Phoenix, AZ. The project consists of two buildings with units ranging in size from 3,300 to 26,700 square feet. Martin, a full-service commercial real estate and construction firm, will serve as an anchor tenant in the development, establishing its regional headquarters within the building to support the firm’s expanding operations and continued growth in the market. Located in Phoenix's Deer Valley industrial submarket along the north I-17 corridor, the development is positioned to serve the growing network of suppliers and service businesses supporting Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s expanding Arizona operations, covering over 2,000 acres and estimated to total around $265 billion. Anna Siradze, Kim Bishop, Will Hainlen and Lauren Maehler led a Talonvest Capital team that arranged the five-year loan, which includes 36 months of interest-only payments, allowing the borrower to complete construction and pursue lease-up before amortization begins. The loan transitions to a 25-year amortization schedule following the interest-only period and includes a declining sliding scale prepayment penalty.
